cards.text: Job is STILL talking. He's remembered the days God watched over him, and now he's in pain and mocked by men younger than he is. So now Job makes his case, and he opens BIG: “I have made a covenant with my eyes.”

cards.question: A covenant with his EYES, friend. Job has made a promise about what he'll look at. What does that promise keep him from doing?

answers.text: Gazing with desire at a virgin
Glaring at the men who mock him
Weeping over all he has lost

cards.text: Then Job fires off questions like a man who already knows every answer: what is a man's heritage from the Almighty on high, and doesn't disaster come to the unjust?

cards.question: Job asks one more question about God and his own ways. Job says God isn't paying attention to the way he lives.

cards.text: Now Job starts a pattern, and he rides it all the way to the end: if he's walked in falsehood, let God weigh him with honest scales. Friend, I HIDE from scales, and this man is ASKING for one.

cards.question: Job asks God to weigh him on honest scales so that God may know his ___.

cards.text: If his steps turned from the path, or his heart followed his eyes, or impurity stuck to his hands, then may another eat what he's sown and may his crops be uprooted.

cards.question: Job keeps saying it: if I did this wrong thing, then let this trouble come on me. What is Job really doing?

cards.text: Next on the list, Job goes there: if his heart was ever enticed by his neighbor's wife, or he lurked at his neighbor's door, then may his own wife grind grain for another, and may other men sleep with her. Whew. Job is not holding ANYTHING back.

cards.question: Job says chasing his neighbor's wife would be a heinous ___, an iniquity to be judged.
Job says that sin is a fire that burns all the way down to Abaddon. What would that fire root out?

cards.text: Then Job brings up his servants: what if one of them had a complaint against him, and he rejected it? Every boss says “my door is always open,” but Job is talking about actually LISTENING.

cards.question: If Job had rejected his servants' complaints, what moment does he say he couldn't face?
Job says the One who made him in the womb also made his servants.

cards.text: Then Job brings up the poor, the widow and the fatherless: what if he denied the poor, let a widow's eyes fail, or ate his morsel alone and never shared it with the fatherless? Friend, I eat a whole batch by myself some nights, but I'm the only one on my planet, so I'm calling that a technicality.

cards.question: Job says he has cared for the fatherless and the widow ever since he was young.

cards.text: Then Job asks what if he saw a needy man with no cloak, and that man's heart never blessed him for warming him with the fleece of his sheep.

cards.question: Job asks what if he lifted his hand against the fatherless because he saw he had support in the ___.
If Job ever lifted his hand against the fatherless, what does he say should happen to him?

answers.text: May his arm fall from his shoulder

cards.question: Job says calamity from God doesn't frighten him.

cards.text: Then Job gets to money: what if he trusted in gold, called pure gold his security, or rejoiced in his great wealth? Friend, I LITERALLY stand on gold, and even I know it can't hold me up.

cards.question: Job asks what if he rejoiced in his great wealth because his own ___ had gained so much.

cards.text: Next, Job looks up at the sky. What if he beheld the sun in its radiance or the moon moving in splendor, and his heart was secretly enticed, and his hand threw a kiss from his mouth?

cards.question: Job says a heart secretly enticed by the sun and moon would be an iniquity to be judged. Why?

answers.text: He would have denied God on high
He would have broken a promise to his friends
He would have forgotten the needy

cards.text: Then Job asks: what if he rejoiced when his enemy was ruined? Friend, the dead batteries I shared that drawer with used to CHEER every time another battery went flat.

cards.question: Job says he asked for his enemy's life with a curse.

cards.text: Then Job brings up his own household. What if the men of his house never said, “Who is there who has not had his fill?”

cards.question: Job says no stranger had to lodge on the street, because his door was open to the ___.

cards.text: What if Job covered his transgressions like Adam, the first man, by hiding his guilt in his heart? Friend, I spent YEARS hidden in the back of a drawer, and trust me, nothing gets better back there.

cards.question: Job describes someone hiding his guilt, staying silent and not going outside. What reason does Job give for hiding like that?

cards.text: Then Job breaks off right in the middle of his list. “Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature.”

cards.question: After signing his name to everything he's said, Job wants the Almighty to stay silent.
Job says let his accuser write up the charges against him. What would Job do with those charges?
Job says he would give account of all his steps and come before God like a prince.

cards.text: Then Job jumps right back into his list: what if his land cries out against him and its furrows weep together? Friend, when a man lets the DIRT testify, you know he's sure of himself.

cards.question: Job asks what if he devoured his land's produce without ___ or broke the spirit of its tenants.
Job's last curse on himself, if he's guilty: what does he want to happen to his fields?

cards.text: And then: “Thus conclude the words of Job.” He has said everything he's got, friend, but this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 12 quotes "my door is always open", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The opening card recaps facts from the passage before this one: Job remembering the days God watched over him (Job 29:2), his pain (Job 30:16-17) and being mocked by younger men (Job 30:1). The card gives no reference for any of them and cites only Job 31:1.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: "So now Job makes his case" presents his pain and the mockery as the reason he makes his case. The text never gives that link between Job 30 and Job 31.

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: "Chasing his neighbor's wife" goes beyond the text. Job 31:9 says his heart was "enticed by my neighbor's wife" or he "lurked at his door." It never says he chased her.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question says "that sin," which points back to a card the baker can no longer see. It never says which sin.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The joke "I LITERALLY stand on gold, and even I know it can't hold me up" contradicts itself. His gold base literally does hold him up, so the line is more likely to confuse a baker than make them laugh.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The joke invents something new about his drawer friends: the batteries cheering every time another battery went flat. The backstory only has them arguing over who had the most charge left. The new detail also turns friends he remembers fondly into gloaters.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The comparison has a different action from the verse. Job 31:33 is about covering transgressions and hiding guilt. Papa Dorin was put away in the drawer and hid no guilt. "Nothing gets better back there" also clashes with his backstory, where he found purpose welcoming newcomers to the drawer.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "Adam, the first man" is a Bible fact from outside the passage, and the card gives no reference for it (for example Genesis 2:7 or 1 Corinthians 15:45).

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.
